rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figures 5-9 - the authors built a 310 g fluorescence LIDAR, mounted it on a DJI Matrice 200 quadcopter and flew it over a ~50 m x 100 m maize plot near Semenovskoe (Moscow region) on 24 June, 17 August and 27 September 2021, reporting their own 680/740 nm chlorophyll fluorescence ratio maps.
rows.notes: The study is a primary instrument-development and feasibility test. It reports only that the drone-borne fluorescence LIDAR can map the 680/740 nm chlorophyll signal over a maize field, that the signal is spatially non-uniform and rises through the season, and that spots of possibly stressed plants can be located. It does not measure yield, productivity, resource-use efficiency, inputs saved or any sustainability outcome; the statements that fast detection 'would allow the prevention of possible crop losses' and that the tool is good for assessing growth and health status are assertions of potential, not results. The study therefore supports only a precondition (stress detection/mapping) of the claimed effect (enhanced productivity and resource-use efficiency), so Q2 is no and upstream is set. Note also that the LIDAR here is a fluorescence (spectroscopic) LIDAR rather than the ranging/point-cloud LiDAR usually meant in productivity claims, though it is still a UAV LiDAR sensor, so technology_mismatch is not flagged. No validation against ground chlorophyll or yield measurements, no replication across sites or crops, no stated limitations beyond daylight interference (measurements had to be made 1-2 h before sunset), and only a 10-shot reproducibility band on one spectrum (Figure 5), which does not pertain to the claimed effect.
